_notes: Coping skills adapted from Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), developed by Marsha Linehan. Original plain-language wording. Skills are reminders, not a substitute for learning DBT with a clinician. TIPP's temperature and intense-exercise steps are intentionally left out for safety.
intro: Quick skills for when feelings start to run high. They come from Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), plus a few simple grounding exercises. Pick one, take your time, and come back to them whenever you need.

learnMore.text: These are reminders, not therapy. DBT and CBT work best when you learn them with a trained clinician.

groups.title: Ground myself in the here and now
Get through the next few minutes

skills.name: STOP
skills.tagline: Hit pause before you do something you'll regret.
skills.when: When you feel an urge to snap, send that text, or storm off.

steps.d: Freeze for a second. Don't move, don't speak, don't type. You're in charge here, not the feeling.
Step away, even just in your head. Take one slow, deep breath.
Notice what's happening inside and around you. What are you feeling? What's actually going on?
Ask yourself what would help most right now, and what you want to happen. Then choose your next move on purpose.

skills.tagline: Use your senses to come back to right now.
skills.when: When your mind is racing or you feel far away from what's around you.

steps.d: Look around and name five things. Really notice them: the color, the shape, a scuff or a pattern.
Your feet on the floor, the chair at your back, the fabric of your sleeve, the air on your skin.
A fan, traffic, a bird, the hum of the fridge. Sounds outside your body count most.
Coffee, soap, fresh air. If nothing's nearby, take a short walk to find a scent.
What's in your mouth right now? Gum, coffee, toothpaste. Or take a sip of water and notice it.

source.name: University of Rochester Medical Center: 5-4-3-2-1 Coping Technique

skills.name: Color hunt
skills.tagline: Find five things of one color.
skills.when: When you need something simple to focus on, anywhere.

steps.d: Start with blue. Any color works.
Look around and name five blue things, out loud or in your head.
For each one, name the exact shade. Not just blue: navy, sky, teal, denim.
Now try red, then green, then yellow. Keep going until you feel steadier.

skills.name: Categories game
skills.tagline: Give your busy mind a small, easy job.
skills.when: When worries keep looping and you can't get out of your head.

steps.d: Dog breeds, cities, foods, movies, sports teams. Something easy and neutral.

steps.t: Name as many as you can
steps.d: Take your time. There's no wrong answer and no timer.
Try one for each letter: apple, banana, carrot... Skip letters that are hard.
When one category runs dry, pick another. Keep going until your mind feels quieter.

skills.name: Paced breathing
skills.tagline: Slow your breath to slow your body down.
skills.when: When your heart is racing or your chest feels tight.

steps.d: Sit or stand comfortably. Let your shoulders drop.
Breathe in through your nose for about 4 counts. Let your belly rise.
Breathe out slowly for about 6 counts, like you're blowing on hot soup. A longer out-breath tells your body it's safe.
Repeat for one to two minutes. If counting feels like too much, just make each out-breath a little longer than the in-breath.

skills.name: Paired muscle relaxation
skills.tagline: Tense, then let go, and let your body follow.
skills.when: When stress is sitting in your shoulders, jaw, or hands.

steps.d: Start with your hands, shoulders, or face. Wherever you're holding tension.
Breathe in and gently tighten that area for about 5 seconds. Firm, not painful.
Breathe out, let it all go, and quietly say "relax" to yourself. Notice the difference.
Work your way through a few areas. Over time, the word "relax" alone can help your body let go.

skills.name: Self-soothe with your senses
skills.tagline: Comfort yourself one sense at a time.
skills.when: When you feel raw and need to be gentle with yourself.

steps.d: Look at something calming: the sky, a favorite photo, a candle, a plant.
Put on soothing music, nature sounds, or a voice you love.
Breathe in something pleasant: coffee, a lotion, fresh air, a favorite soap.
Slowly sip a warm drink or savor a small treat. Really taste it.
Wrap up in a soft blanket, pet an animal, or hold something with a comforting texture.

skills.name: ACCEPTS
skills.tagline: Distract yourself until the wave passes.
skills.when: When a feeling is strong and you can't fix the problem right now.

steps.d: Do something that takes some focus: a walk, a puzzle, cleaning, a show.
Help someone. Send a kind message, do a favor, or volunteer.
Remember a time you got through something hard. You've coped before.
Bring in a different feeling on purpose: a funny video, an uplifting song.
Set the problem aside for now. Picture putting it in a box on a high shelf. You can come back to it later.
Give your mind a job: count backward from 100 by 7s, name things in a category, or read.
Shift your focus with a gentle sensation: a warm shower, a good stretch, a strong mint.

skills.name: IMPROVE the moment
skills.tagline: Make a hard moment a little more bearable.
skills.when: When you're stuck in a tough situation you can't leave.

steps.d: Picture a calm, safe place in detail. What do you see, hear, and feel there?
Look for any purpose or lesson in this, even a small one.
Pray, meditate, or connect with whatever brings you peace.
Loosen your body. Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, breathe slowly.
Focus fully on just what you're doing right now. Only this step.
Take a short break: five minutes outside, a cup of tea, closing your eyes.
Talk to yourself like a good friend would: "I can get through this. This won't last forever."

skills.name: DEAR MAN
skills.tagline: Ask for what you need, clearly and kindly.
skills.when: When you need to make a request or say no.

steps.d: Stick to the facts of the situation. No blaming.
Share how you feel about it, using "I feel..." statements.
Ask for what you want, or say no, clearly. Don't make them guess.
Explain how it helps them too, or thank them when they come through.
Stay on topic. If the conversation drifts, calmly come back to your point.
Steady voice, eye contact, good posture. Even if you don't feel it yet.
Be willing to give a little. Ask, "What would work for you?"

skills.name: GIVE
skills.tagline: Keep the relationship strong while you talk.
skills.when: When the relationship matters as much as getting your way.

steps.d: No attacks, threats, or judging. Keep your tone kind.
Listen to their side. Let them finish.
Show you understand how they feel, even if you disagree.
A little warmth or humor goes a long way. Smile if it fits.

skills.name: FAST
skills.tagline: Keep your self-respect in a tough conversation.
skills.when: When you're tempted to give in just to keep the peace.

steps.d: Be fair to the other person, and to yourself.
Don't over-apologize for having needs or opinions.
Don't trade away what matters to you to avoid conflict.
Be honest. No exaggerating, no making excuses.

skills.name: Catch it, check it, change it
skills.tagline: Question an unhelpful thought instead of believing it.
skills.when: When a thought is dragging your mood down.

steps.d: Notice the thought and say it to yourself in words: "I'm thinking that..."
Is it a fact or a guess? What's the evidence for it, and against it? Would you say this to a friend?
Swap it for something more balanced and kind. It doesn't have to be cheerful, just fair and true.

skills.name: Spot the thinking trap
skills.tagline: Name the trap, and it loosens its grip.
skills.when: When your thoughts feel extreme or stuck on the worst.

steps.d: Get it out of your head and into words.
Common ones: all-or-nothing, expecting the worst, mind reading, predicting the future, "shoulds," labeling yourself, ignoring the good, and "I feel it, so it must be true."
"That's mind reading." Just naming it puts a little space between you and the thought.
Rewrite the thought without the trap. "I always mess up" might become "I made a mistake today, and I've done plenty right too."

skills.name: Worst, best, most likely
skills.tagline: Zoom out from the worst-case story.
skills.when: When your mind jumps straight to disaster.

steps.d: What's the worst that could realistically happen? Say it plainly.
If it did happen, what would you do? Who could help? You've handled hard things before.
What's the best that could happen? Let yourself picture it.
Somewhere in between is what usually happens. What's the most likely outcome?

skills.name: Thought record
skills.tagline: Walk through a tough moment on paper.
skills.when: When you have a few minutes and want to untangle what happened.

steps.d: What happened? Where were you, and who was there? Just the facts.
What did you feel, and how strong was it, from 0 to 100?
What went through your mind? Which thought hit the hardest?
What facts back that thought up?
What facts don't fit? What would a friend point out?
Put the evidence together into a fairer way to see it.
How strong is the feeling now, from 0 to 100? Any change counts.

skills.name: Check the facts
skills.tagline: Make sure the feeling fits what's really happening.
skills.when: When your reaction feels bigger than the situation.

steps.d: Describe just the facts, like a camera would see it.
Notice the meaning you're adding. What are you assuming?
Think of at least one other way to see it.
Does this feeling, and how strong it is, match the facts? If not, it's okay to let some of it go.

skills.name: Opposite action
skills.tagline: When a feeling doesn't fit, act the opposite way.
skills.when: When an emotion is pushing you toward something that won't help.

steps.d: Fear, anger, sadness, shame? Put a name on it.
What does it want you to do? Hide, yell, stay in bed?
Does acting on this urge help you right now? If not, try the opposite.

steps.t: Do the opposite, all the way
steps.d: Fear says avoid, so approach a little. Sadness says withdraw, so get moving or reach out. Anger says attack, so step away and be kind.

skills.name: Wise mind
skills.tagline: Find the middle between feeling and thinking.
skills.when: When you're torn between what you feel and what you think.

steps.d: What are your feelings telling you to do?
What do the facts and logic say?
Take a slow breath. As you breathe out, let your attention settle in your center.
Quietly ask, "What's the wise thing to do here?" Wait for an answer that feels calm and true.

skills.name: One small step
skills.tagline: Do first, and let the mood catch up.
skills.when: When you feel low, flat, or can't get started.

steps.d: Choose one activity that's enjoyable or gives you a sense of getting something done. Smaller is better.
"Clean the kitchen" can become "wash five dishes." No step is too small.
Decide when you'll do it, like "after lunch" or "at 4 PM."
Afterward, notice how you feel, even if the change is tiny. You don't have to feel motivated first.

skills.name: Problem solving
skills.tagline: Turn a big mess into one next step.
skills.when: When a real, practical problem feels overwhelming.

steps.d: Describe it in one or two sentences, focusing on facts, not blame.
Write down all the ideas, even the silly ones. Don't judge them yet.
For the most promising ones, jot down the pros and cons.
Choose a solution and break it into small, specific steps.
Give it a go. If it didn't work, that's information. Go back and try another option.

skills.name: Worry time
skills.tagline: Give worries an appointment instead of your whole day.
skills.when: When worries keep popping up and taking over.

steps.d: Pick 10 to 15 minutes later today for worrying, not too close to bedtime.
When a worry shows up, jot it down and tell yourself, "I'll think about this at worry time."
Return to what you were doing. The worry is saved. You don't have to hold it.
At worry time, look at your list. Some worries won't matter anymore. For the rest, ask if there's anything you can do.

skills.name: Face it, one step at a time
skills.tagline: Build courage with small, steady steps.
skills.when: When you've been avoiding something because it makes you anxious.

steps.d: Pick one thing anxiety has been keeping you from doing.
List small steps from easiest to hardest. Each one a little more challenging than the last.
Try the easiest step. Stay with it until the anxiety starts to ease, even a little.
Repeat a step until it feels manageable, then move up. Going slowly still counts.

skills.name: PLEASE
skills.tagline: Take care of your body so feelings are easier to handle.
skills.when: Every day. Strong feelings hit harder when your body is run down.

steps.d: Take care of aches, pain, and illness. See a doctor when you need to.
Eat regular meals, not too much and not too little.
Go easy on alcohol and other substances that can throw off your mood.
Aim for enough sleep, on a regular schedule.
Move your body most days, even a short walk.
